item.title: For 50 Years, Did We Only Measure What's Wrong With Men?
item.description:
Relationships

For 50 Years, Did We Only Measure What's Wrong With Men?

A scoping review of research reveals what masculinity measures have left out.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • The academic world has long focused on the risks and harms associated with masculine norms.
  • The results sections of academic papers on masculinity can feel like foregone conclusions about masculinity.
  • Most masculinity measures adopted a more deficit-based approach; but 22 percent incorporated strengths-based.
  • Movember's scholarship points to a new direction in measuring masculinity that incorporates more complexity.

At the start of my doctoral training in clinical psychology in the 2010s, as one of the few men in my program, I was drawn to what academics had to say about me—that is, about men and masculinity. In discussions, it was common to highlight the harms of masculinity. Articulating the strengths, the mosaic of traits and cultural variation that also compose masculinity risked sounding out-of-touch, or worse, opposed to the ascent of women and girls.

Even if I had tried to add more nuance, the lives of men I knew seemed too vast and contradictory; I struggled to define masculinity satisfyingly.

In training, there was no shortage of masculinity-related measures to peruse, from the classic Bem Sex Role Inventory (1974) and the Male Role Norms Inventory (1992) to the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory (2003). Some more recent ones in the 2010s seemed culturally attuned, attentive to male relationships, or offered respondents the ability to self-define masculinity. Still, most hovered around gender role strain, a foundational theory that the pressure to live up to how a man should be is central to what causes men psychological harm.

For instance, the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory is organized around categories ranging from emotional control, winning, playboy, and violence to self-reliance, risk-taking, power over women, and primacy of work. Items to endorse, or reject, read something like this:

"I never share my feelings."

"I hate asking for help."

I could recognize some of myself in these items, my pals, my dad, Uncle Jeff, to some degree, but did they richly capture our camaraderie and cultural nuances? The all-nighters, early mornings, the ribbing and rituals, the unblinking care without labeling it “care”?

Source: Kaboompics / Pexels

Traditional Masculinity

The results sections of academic papers felt foregone. Pick a harmful outcome—substance misuse, restricted emotion, poor heart health—and greater adherence to "traditional masculine norms" would be linked to worse results, like a glitching Magic 8 ball only predicting doom.

The scales seemed pre-tipped in a way that missed the ordinary theater of male existence: a dad brushing his daughter’s tangled hair as she yelps in protest, then refreshing an app to make sure her summer-camp deposit went through; the buddy who takes four subway trains across two hours to help you move apartments; the dad who has never uttered “I love you,” but whose head-lock hug articulates a marrow-deep love.

Many academic measures have converged on the construct of "traditional masculinity ideology," put forth by Ronald Levant and flagged as potentially harmful in the APA's 2018 Guidelines for Psychological Practice with Boys and Men. Traditional masculinity scholarship often fixates on restrictive emotionality, avoidance of femininity, toughness, aggression, self-reliance, achievement and status, sex without intimacy, and negativity toward sexual minorities.

The above norms, which I'll label the 'Loudest Eight' of masculinity, have value, are revealing, yet suck the air out of conversations on masculinity. They are the noisiest bunch under a much bigger masculinity tent.

Later in my training, as I began treating male clients, I couldn’t just intellectualize masculinity. What I witnessed defied those questionnaires: Olympic-level performances of fine and fiercely devoted stay-at-home dads, guys self-reliant and unhealthily dependent on women, men capable of surgical sensitivity and reckless rage.

Yet consuming each new publication on masculinity left me with the nagging sense that something essential was missing.

Balanced Masculinity

It was later that I found hope in a 2010 paper by Kiselica and Englar-Carlson introducing the Positive Psychology-Positive Masculinity paradigm (PPPM). It offered an inspiring version of masculinity organized around: male relational styles, male ways of caring, generative fatherhood, self-reliance, the worker-provider tradition, courage and worthwhile risk, the group orientation of boys and men, humanitarian service, humor, and heroism. This seemed no match for decades of research telling a more cautionary tale.

So I was eager to read a recent 2026 scoping review, a map of the measurement terrain, from the team at the Movember Institute of Men's Health. Published in Men and Masculinities, it is titled What Is the Measure of a Man? A Systematic Scoping Review of 50 Years of Masculinities Scales.

The review suggests that, as a field, we have too often built tools to measure what is wrong with men, losing sight of the strengths-based, culturally varied, and relationship-oriented dimensions of masculinity. The review examined 65 masculinity measures created between 1974 and 2024. Seventy-eight percent of the measures took a deficit-based approach, generally built on the expectation that greater measured masculinity would be associated with worse outcomes. Only 22 percent incorporated strengths-based elements.

Researchers sorted the measures into one of two buckets: Deficit, as in "A real man never shows emotion." Or, strengths, as in "Men show strength in various ways, including displaying vulnerability." To land in the strengths bucket, a scale only had to include some positive framing. A single positive subscale could tip an entire measure over into a strength measure; to be called deficit-based, a scale had to be thoroughly organized around negative outcomes.

Strengths were easier to earn and deficits harder; even so, 78 percent of measures still came out as deficits.

Here's what else caught my attention: the measures published before 2000 make up less than a third of the sample yet draw over three-quarters of all citations. This is a reminder that social scientists, myself included, have turned our attention to this deficit frame eagerly and often.

This paper adds scholarship to what I could only frustratingly observe in my training. The missing dimensions were never absent from the men I knew. The measures captured only part of the picture. As the review noted, sometimes measures did not even make clear whether a respondent in a study was describing what he actually believed, what he thought other men believed, or just the mandates of manhood he’d inhaled across a lifetime that he knew were still in the ether.

The dad wielding a hairbrush, the buddy ready to break his back for you, the guy full of love with no words for it. These are the men I sit across from trying, imperfectly, to live meaningful lives. I hope this new paper helps re-tip academia’s scales toward that complexity, toward masculinities that bind and build as much as those that disconnect and dominate.

item.title: When Is Two Hours of TV After School Good Parenting?
item.description:
Parenting

When Is Two Hours of TV After School Good Parenting?

Responsive parenting isn't just about following one-size-fits-all advice.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Today's over-saturated world of parenting guidance, espousing rigid dictates, can be harmful to families.
  • They don't take into consideration the unique characteristics and needs of the child.
  • This has harmed parents who know their child needs something the "experts" are deeming harmful.
  • There is no one-size-fits-all approach to child-rearing. The science can be adapted to the individual child.

Harry, 7, came home from school every day a complete mess. It was one explosion after another. Total stress and chaos. No chance for connection or joy as a family. His mom, Kristen, had tried everything: she stayed calm; she tried to talk to him about his feelings; she tried a range of strategies to help him calm down. Nothing worked. Most strategies backfired, increasing Harry’s dysregulation.

Kristen took a step back and reflected on what she knows about Harry: He is a very sensitive and intense child, and by the end of a long day at school, he is fried. He has far surpassed his threshold for coping and needs to zone out completely. The screen provides that.

She was trying to stick to the limit of 60 minutes a day, based on what her pediatrician and popular parenting accounts had deemed the maximum, lest you harm your child. However, her thoughtful assessment of Harry told her it wasn’t sufficient. He needed more time. While conflicted, Kristen started letting Harry watch up to two straight hours of only appropriate content before dinner.

The outcome

After the two hours of TV, for the rest of the night, Harry is a total delight—calm and content. They now have lovely evenings filled with connection and (minimal) chaos. Sensitive, responsive, not “permissive” parenting tunes in to your child and makes thoughtful decisions about what they need to maximize healthy functioning—whatever that looks like for them.

The point of this story is not to let your child watch two straight hours a day. Your decisions about screen time and every other facet of your child’s life should be informed by science and adapted to your child's unique needs.

To do that, consider the impact of your response.

If what you're doing helps your child build skills and cope more effectively over time, it's supportive.

If what you're doing helps your child avoid developing those skills—especially because you're trying to prevent a tantrum by lowering expectations they can actually meet—it's more likely to be enabling.

Take the screen time dilemma

For Harry, this decision was supportive because he was able to participate in family dinner, get through bedtime tasks, and enjoy reading and cuddle time. In the cost-benefit analysis this mom made, there was way more benefit.

For another child, letting them watch two consecutive hours of TV every day may be enabling. They can come home after school and engage with friends, play on their own, or participate in an extracurricular because their system is not overloaded. But they would prefer to sit in front of a screen for hours and so beg for that. Acquiescing in that case may be enabling, as it's a missed opportunity for that child to experience more fortifying activities.

Perhaps the most important take-homes for me from this story

1) There is no one-size-fits-all approach to child-rearing. Rigid dictates have been very harmful to the families I work with who have highly reactive children. In addition to feeling harshly judged for their child’s often outsized and seemingly irrational behavior, they often feel like their hands are tied because what they instinctively know their child needs is counter to popular, “accepted” parenting practices.

2) Don’t judge a parent until you’ve walked in their shoes.

item.title: When Shoes Don’t Fit, We Change the Shoes, Not the Feet
item.description:
Environment

When Shoes Don’t Fit, We Change the Shoes, Not the Feet

Here's a better way to look at people-environment mismatches.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Only individuals know when shoes fit the way they want.
  • When someone doesn’t fit in a particular environment, we could change the environment rather than the person.
  • Organizing environments so that everyone can achieve what they want is ideal.
Source: asphoto777 / 123RF

Do you remember the last time you bought a pair of shoes? Maybe you saw some you liked, tried them on, walked around in them, looked at them in the mirror, and then decided whether to buy them.

Some people might not do all of those things. Other people might do more. Perhaps the size isn’t quite right, so you ask for the next size up or down.

Of course, what you want the shoes for will affect what’s important. If you’re running a half marathon, you will want certain things. But if you’re working on a construction site, different features will matter. And if you want to make a dreamy impression on a romantic first date, other things entirely will be important.

When shoes aren’t right for whatever reason, we do things to correct that. If they’re a bit tight, we get a bigger size. If they’re too loose, we get a smaller size. If they’re the wrong color or style, we look for different ones.

This is all just a long-winded way of saying that when there’s a mismatch between shoes and feet, we change the shoes, not the feet. Salespeople in shoe stores don’t advise customers to get corrective surgery so that the shoes they want to sell will fit. They look for other shoes.

We don’t blame the foot if the shoe doesn’t fit.

But if we think about a shoe as the environment a foot occupies, in other situations, we do the opposite.

Source: seventyfour74 / 123RF

Take schools, for example. If students don’t fit the environment of a classroom or school, we often conclude that there’s something wrong with the student. Perhaps at first, changes are made to classes, subjects, or schools. Ultimately, though, if the mismatch between student and school continues, it is the student who is blamed.

The blaming takes different forms but usually results in the young person being labeled or diagnosed in some way. The thinking is that the young person is the one with the problem. They are somehow deficient and need to be “fixed.”

The “blaming” is often well-meaning. Many people sincerely want to help when they see young people struggling in different situations. The tendency, though, is almost always to expect the youngster to change, not the environment.

article continues after advertisement

And it doesn’t just happen with young people. I was recently at a meeting of health and other professionals in my town. One of the topics we talked about was how some services were not being used very much. The ideas that were offered to fix this were different ways of engaging people and persuading them to use the services more. No one raised the idea that perhaps these services were not priorities for this community. Again, the focus was on changing the people, not the environment.

It’s also true that some people do want to change things about themselves. Maybe they can’t decide on an important life decision. Do they stay or go? Do they speak up or stay quiet? Counseling and psychotherapy can be extremely useful in helping people explore and resolve inner turmoil and conflict.

But deciding what needs to change can only ever be personally determined. No one can tell someone else what the best solution is for them. Only you know if the shoe fits—other people can’t tell you that. If it doesn’t fit, it doesn’t fit regardless of what others might think.

And trying to change yourself in the context of a difficult environment is not likely to be successful for very long. If someone is experiencing workplace bullying and harassment, letting them know about counseling services will not be very helpful. At least not in any ongoing way. In this situation, it is the environment that needs changing. The bullying and harassment must be stopped.

We pay a lot of attention to the way people conduct themselves. We need to pay just as much attention to the environments within which that conduct occurs. Maybe even more attention. Changing people will not create a better fit between people and places.

Comfortable environments are good for all, but comfort is only ever personally defined. My comfort might be your chaos. My neat and tidy might feel constraining to you.

But places can be designed with enough options for people to create their own comfort without preventing others from doing the same. When we recognize people as controllers, those kinds of places will be as common as shoe stores (Marken & Carey, 2015).

To make the world a better place for all, we don’t need to walk a mile, or any other distance, in another person’s shoes. Harmony and cohesion will be widespread when we have places where we can all walk wherever we want, for as long as we want, in the way we want.

article continues after advertisement

Where will your walking take you?

item.title: The Real Reason You Fall Apart Under Pressure
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

The Real Reason You Fall Apart Under Pressure

You think staying calm under pressure is a personality trait. You're wrong.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Falling apart under pressure isn't a character flaw. It's a skill gap.
  • In a recent study, 15 hours of emotion-regulation training nearly doubled soldiers' accuracy under stress.
  • Your flinch was trained in childhood, which is why "just stay calm" can never fix it.

You knew the material cold and went blank in the interview anyway. You promised yourself you wouldn’t yell and heard your voice rise on the second sentence. You walked into your boss’s office with three important asks and walked out having asked for... none.

We’ve all been there.

Most of us draw the same conclusion: I’m just not built for pressure.

If that’s your story, a study published this year in Scientific Reports disagrees.

Under acute stress (being-shot-at-while-tying-a-tourniquet sort of stress), one group of elite soldiers hit 94.1 percent of their shooting targets. A second group (same job, same skills) hit 51.6 percent. The difference? Fifteen hours of training in something most driven people dismiss as a soft skill: noticing, understanding, and managing emotions, both their own and others’.

And it wasn’t just shooting that improved. The trained group also got better at math and memorization! Clearer memory, faster thinking, lower biological stress.

Want this too?

The Story You’ve Been Telling Yourself About Pressure

I believed the trait story for years. I was certain that people who handled life without needing to escape stress, through drinking or some other troubling habit, were built differently. Two decades of self-work, research, and clinical work have shown me what that belief does. Because if composure is a trait, then falling apart is a self-directed verdict.

This study says otherwise. When your alarm fires, experiencing a threat, a craving, or a hard conversation, your body pulls resources away from what you need most: working memory, fine motor control, and flexible thinking. Think about it: you didn’t go blank in the interview because the answers weren’t there. The part of you that held them was walled off from access.

Pressure moments are training sessions. When you flee or numb the feeling, you’re practicing the flinch, which makes it more likely to return.

Imagine it’s 9:40 on a Tuesday: you’ve read the same report summary three times, you snap at your kid, and by 10, you’re standing in the refrigerator light, not hungry (but reaching for the ice cream). Year by year, the menu of what you can face quietly narrows, until it looks, from the inside, exactly like “just who I am.”

Why “Just Stay Calm” Has Never Worked

You’ve heard the advice: just breathe, stay calm, don’t take it personally.

If that advice were sufficient, you’d be all good by now.

It fails because it ignores where your alarm response was trained. I call these hooks: the hidden emotional drivers that created this pattern and keep it running long after it stops serving you. Here’s how they came about (importantly, you don’t control this):

1. You learned that feelings were fires. In many homes, big emotions are emergencies. Anger got you sent to your room; tears got you “something to cry about.” You learned that safety returns when the feeling stops. It was the right choice then, when you had no other tools. But it didn’t teach you to swim; it taught you to get the hell out of the water. Pressure keeps throwing you back in.

2. You learned that composure was currency. Maybe you were the easy one, the kid who didn’t add problems. Approval arrived when you looked calm, so you got brilliant at looking calm, always. But your heart was hammering away. It looked like composure, but it was performance. The panic went underground, where nobody could coach it and where it keeps detonating decades later.

3. You copied the only reps on display. Kids learn regulation by watching what the big people do when they get flooded. If your model was a father who left the room or a mother who poured a drink every evening after work, escape wasn’t a flaw you developed. It was the family MO. You inherited the flinch the way you inherited your last name.

Trace any of these back, and the behavior makes sense. It protected you when you had nothing better. It just doesn’t serve you now. Reps got you in. Reps will get you out.

What Retraining Looks Like

A client I’ll call Marcus was eight months into the work, convinced he had a discipline problem. He was practicing and doing pretty well, but when the CEO expressed frustration with a deliverable, or he got called out in a presentation, he’d lapse right back into an all-nighter weekend. Every time, the same conclusion: I’m weak.

Marcus was getting hopeless that he could never change (as was his team).

But Marcus didn’t have a discipline problem on the weekend. He had an emotional regulation problem in the conference room—when his performance was being questioned, his mind and body screamed at him, “I told you you’re a failure!” The all-nighters (with a few stiff drinks to boot) weren’t the failure. They were the rebound reaction for a state he’d never learned to move through. An athlete in his youth, with a demanding father who expected perfection, Marcus learned to go all-in no matter what. His keep-going-at-all-costs work marathons were a replay of his past attempts to prove to his father that he really was worthy of love.

We stopped practicing refusal and started practicing regulation and self-worth.

The work was learning to identify and downshift before making any decisions. The first night it worked was almost anticlimactic: same conference room commentary, same heat in his chest, but after 30 seconds of naming it and slowing his exhale in the restroom, the feeling crested and came down on its own. He watched it recede, went inside, and kept going.

That night, and over the weekend, he was able to be a father and a husband.

The cravings didn’t vanish. They just lost their authority.

Your First Reps

Fifteen hours is what it took in the study. You probably spend more than that on scrolling every week. What if, instead, you spent those hours learning to manage internal states?!

Three times—before a meeting, mid-moment, and after a difficult experience—pause for 30 to 90 seconds, and then do this:

  1. Notice where the activation lives in your body. Chest? Jaw? Stomach? Find it, literally. Put a hand on the spot. Don’t run away. Lean in.
  2. Name the feeling in one or two words, out loud or on paper. Be precise. Not “stressed,” but “I’m feeling humiliated,” or “I’m afraid.” Naming turns something happening to you into something you’re watching. Name it to tame it.
  3. Slow one thing down. Take four or five breaths with the exhale running twice as long as the inhale. This turns up your parasympathetic nervous system, letting it know the threat has passed. Parking lot, driveway, hallway, restroom—the rep counts anywhere.

Up to 90 seconds, three times a day. Your off-ramp from the most stressful moments can be built from repeating exactly these reps.

Remember This

You are always training something in pressure moments—the flinch or the skill. Your old reps helped you survive an old threat; the new ones are an active choice for the life you want to live. These reps start working in weeks and compound over months. If you keep practicing, you’ll find yourself amazed at the powerful emotion-regulating muscles you’ll build. So go ahead and take your reps badly at first, on purpose.

Which pressure moment are you going to practice this week?

For more on the hidden drivers behind persistent patterns, see my book Unhooked.

item.title: Was Madame Butterfly a Victim or a Young Woman With Agency?
item.description:
Media

Was Madame Butterfly a Victim or a Young Woman With Agency?

A Personal Perspective: Psychological themes of a popular opera.

Posted July 15, 2026

Karen Chia-ling Ho as Madama Butterfly
Source: Bronwen Sharp for the Santa Fe Opera

You likely have heard of Madame Butterfly, the main character in one of the most famous operas ever composed: Madame Butterfly by Giacomo Puccini with his librettists Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa. Opera goers often make sure they have tissues or handkerchiefs with them, and they sigh softly in their seats as the music soars to a dramatic crescendo and the story moves to its tragic end.

It takes place in Nagasaki, Japan, in the early twentieth century, when a naval officer named Pinkerton arrives in the port on an American ship. He’s a self-admitted player who hooks up with a woman at every stop. This time, a Japanese marriage broker arranges for him to wed a beautiful, young Japanese woman. The contract is as easy to break as it is to sign, and he sings about maybe falling in love but definitely falling in lust with his new young bride, and knowing that his real marriage will one day be to an American woman.

The bride, Cio-Cio San, aka Madame Butterfly, is reluctant to marry Pinkerton because she has heard that American men exploit Japanese women, marry them for convenience, and abandon them, which is legally considered a divorce. But she is smitten with Pinkerton and believes she will be different. She embraces Pinkerton’s American culture, and secretly converts to his Christian religion.

Once she has abandoned the Japanese gods and religion, her relative all turn against her and abandon her. All she has left in the world is Pinkerton and when duty calls, he leaves, promising that he be back soon. Three years pass, and he doesn’t return. Butterfly is impoverished, and may have to go back to being a geisha, singing in the street to entertain people, in order to support the son she has from her marriage to Pinkerton.

The marriage broker has another husband lined up for her, because he knows Pinkerton is not coming back. Her ever-faithful maid Suzuki tells Butterfly that Pinkerton is not returning. The only person sure that he will return is Butterfly. All the evidence clearly shows that Pinkerton has abandoned Butterfly, but the reality is unbearable for her so she acts and lives according to her unfounded belief that he will come back. Sadly, she seems to develop severe cognitive dissonance, which proves to be extremely harmful to her.

Cognitive Dissonance Theory was first introduced by psychologist Leon Festinger in the late 1950s. Saul McLoud, Ph.D., defines it as “the mental discomfort experienced when a person holds two conflicting beliefs or when their actions don’t align with their beliefs. To reduce this uncomfortable feeling, people often change their thoughts or justify their behavior to make everything feel more consistent. For example, when people smoke (behavior), and they know that smoking causes cancer (cognition), they are in a state of cognitive dissonance.”

Pinkerton has even written a letter to his counsel about his new life without Butterfly, but she will not listen to it. She has given up everything for him — her relatives, her religion, her social status as a married woman — and has no fallback position. When Pinkerton finally shows up with his American wife, who offers to raise the child Butterfly had with her husband, Butterfly agrees. She has no money left to raise him, he will be scorned as a bastard, and she knows his life in America will give him opportunity. She sees suicide as the only option for herself. The one belief that kept her going — the return of her husband — was untrue. She cannot bear the reality that faces her. When Pinkerton gets up the nerve to see her, she is a corpse.

People weep when seeing this opera because Butterfly is only 15 years old when she marries Pinkerton, and 18 when she ends her life. She is a young, beautiful, pure, sensitive being who is destroyed by a bogus marriage to a man who represents a chauvinistic, condescending attitude toward Japanese culture and Japanese women — who have been portrayed as submissive victims in some productions of Madame Butterfly. I’ve heard that Japanese people are often offended by the opera.

The Santa Fe Opera hired Melanie Bacaling, a woman, as director, and she said she did not see Butterfly as a victim but, rather, a woman with agency — a woman who made decisions and took things into her own hands. This is an intelligent approach, and she sets out to remove stereotypical depictions of Japanese women, and insists that all American men are not as insensitive and uncaring as Pinkerton. Bacaling emphasizes the compassion of another American man, a counsel, who vigorously opposes Pinkerton’s behavior towards Butterfly.

Is this contemporary spin about agency successful? Not for this viewer. Butterfly is spunky and cautious at first as she has heard much about feckless foreign men. She is a dreamer and a believer in love, and her newfound Western faith and inner strength allow her to trust that her beloved will return as he promised. Once that belief takes hold, nothing will convince Butterfly to challenge or change it.

If she had agency as a feisty young woman who was afraid of being loved and abandoned by a foreign man, it evaporated once she married Pinkerton and believed in his undying love. Her illusion collapses brutally when he arrives with his American wife. Butterfly doesn’t fight to keep her child. She gives in and gives up. She blindfolds her beloved son so he won’t see while she stands near him and thrusts a fateful sword into her heart. Her inability to accept a new reality and give up her beliefs about Pinkerton leads to her self-harm. Does this show agency? Alas, she is a victim of culture, the times, and the prevailing mores. When the singer portraying Pinkerton comes out to take a bow, the audience aggressively boos him. They do something Butterfly could never do.

While many audience members loved the show, others, especially some younger attendees, said the opera was racist, sexist, and presented a view of a woman in a relationship that they couldn’t abide. Other audience members disagreed and said that anyone who has suffered loss, grief, pain in a relationship, or unrequited love would be weeping sympathetically from the story. So would anyone experiencing cognitive dissonance about love or a lover.

So go, watch, admire the performances and voices, listen to Puccini’s romantic music, and see what you feel and think about one of the most frequently performed operas in the world in one of the most dramatic opera houses in the U.S. Is it agency or harmful cognitive dissonance? You can decide.

item.title: Why We Watch the World Cup
item.description:
Identity

Why We Watch the World Cup

Consider the different meanings of the fan experience.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Huge sporting spectacles, like the World Cup, draw millions within the terms of the event.
  • Fans express the wish to be part of something greater than oneself, but they also seek social distinction.
  • Media may guide our encounters with sporting culture, helping us focus on some issues and ignore others.

Sixteen years ago this week, my wife and I arrived in Europe for a short trip that combined work and pleasure. Still groggy from the fight, we were staying at a run-down hotel in Copenhagen, Denmark. The night was warm; the balcony doors were open. Suddenly, groups of people — some dressed in orange, others in red — went marching past the hotel. Thoroughfares jammed, bars came alive. A few minutes later, roars started echoing through the city.

We had, it seems, found ourselves in Europe on the final day of the World Cup. Spain was playing the Netherlands in South Africa. The fact that Denmark had no stake in the distant battle seemed not to matter. Down in the streets, people were, quite literally, showing their colors. Beyond the game, the world had shut down. This moment was the only thing that mattered. The whole affair was thrilling.

A couple of hours later, the shouting was over. Spain had won, 1-0 in “added extra time.” But the sense of eventfulness, the feeling that one was part of an important occasion, remained.

Once again, the World Cup arrives, this time in North America. The final match approaches. More than a billion will watch. This is the case even in the United States, where — and despite the great successes of our national women’s team — most people aren’t soccer fans.

Our men’s team — by standards we’ve grown accustomed to — did well this year, losing to Belgium in the round of 16. More than 50 million Americans watched. Quickly, we learned the names and faces of star players. More slowly, we comprehended rules. With the American team now out of the picture, many of us have picked favorites for the battles that remain.

Why does anyone care? Let’s analyze the World Cup’s — or any huge sporting event’s — appeal.

Wanting to be part of something

As they do with the Super Bowl — the last one drew 125 million American viewers — people wish to participate in great secular holidays. The better-attended the occasion, the more important it seems. Essentially, events like these are excuses to go out or have parties. Ideally, one should be with friends and family; however, similarly disposed strangers may substitute. At the least, one should “have plans” for the viewing.

Having been to numerous occasions of this sort, I can report that many attendees care little about the game. They are there to eat and drink and to participate in the merriment. Everyone knows they should pick and root for a favorite (“Who’s playing again?”). They should expect gentle teasing from the opposing side. Cheering is obligatory. No one should show disrespect for the activity or talk noisily about unrelated matters. Complaining about the game’s ups and downs is welcomed. Complaining about personal matters — perhaps one’s latest surgery — is not.

The point is to be there and to have it known that one was there. This behavior reaches an extreme with those attending the game in-person. There, commitment is measured by seat location (read, pricing) and costuming. Comedians joke that modern people’s highest aspiration is to see their own visage on a Jumbotron. Seeing, and being seen, conjoin.

Ways to gain status

Communal involvement is a wonderful thing. But most of us want ways to show that we are not only part of the group but have advanced standing within it.

Hosting a watch party is one way. Essentials for this are a large and dependable television, suitable gathering space, and ample liquor supply. What is not required is any knowledge of the game beyond starting time and duration. Note too that hosting creates “social debt” and enhances chances for other (perhaps more desirable) involvements in the future.

Mere guests can gain status by educating less knowledgeable others. That may include recounts of previous games played by the teams at hand. Some information about key players (perhaps what club they play for on a “regular” basis) may be passed along.

Critically, in the case of soccer, one can offer easy-to-understand explanations of rules, especially the offside rule. Fouls are mystifying to many Americans, including whether an infraction should merit a yellow or red card. Armed with this knowledge, the newly informed can participate in spirited discussions about a red-carded player’s being banned from a subsequent game (and a US President getting involved) or a reversed yellow-card decision resulting in the heretofore fouled opponent now receiving that punishment himself.

In such ways, the sophisticate emerges. Some individuals document that involvement by tattoos and other bodily marking or brag about games they’ve attended. Some try to prove their skill by gambling.

Nationalism and patriotism

Many writers have described nationalism as a danger in our modern, highly weaponized world. Erich Fromm, for example, called nationalism “our form of incest” and patriotism “its cult.” Surely, nationalism’s aggressive, unbounded forms are scourges.

That said, basic pride in one’s society — its people, history, languages, and lifeways — is a good thing. So is patriotism that moves the person beyond mere selfishness. All of us should respect the many kinds of people who have inhabited our portion of the world and support their collective future. Personal freedom is a collective matter.

The World Cup showcases that commitment. We see players singing (fervently) their national anthems. Flags and banners are everywhere. Fans adorn themselves as cultural characters. When teams lose, tears flow.

The culture of the game

Big events like these appear to “stop time” and impose their own spatial and temporal regimes. For a few hours, we abandon more important concerns. Let us enjoy watching skilled performers do what they themselves clearly enjoy. Such is the charm of play.

The apparent lesson is that regulated competition is beneficial rather than harmful. Rival players embrace and exchange jerseys at game’s end. Sportsmanship is a model for public discourse.

Just because the event is trivial — adults in short pants chasing a ball — it distills human accomplishment. Matters of technique, strategy, and “character” come to the fore. Having played games ourselves, we feel we know what these experts are trying to accomplish. Essentially non-verbal, their activity becomes a universal language that crosses nationality and generation.

Media guides our watching. We are told to think of games as confrontations between star players. Teams have national styles and perhaps “golden generations.” The difficulty of what everyone is doing is emphasized. Losers receive a few moments of consolation and then attention turns to the victor’s next game. History, it seems, is being made and we are part of it.

What we must not do is think about the financial implications of all this, perhaps player contracts and endorsements or costs and disruptions to host cities. Downplay ticket prices, national prejudices, bribery, and other questionable behaviors. Advertise gambling opportunities and odds but feign ignorance of any ensuing problems. Attention must stay within the publicly acknowledged frame.

A sports fan myself, I acknowledge these are general implications of high-profile celebrity culture, where certain occasions — and certain people — are given much attention and others are kept in the shadows. But like theater audiences of very sort, we give ourselves to the spectacle that unfolds before us. And we are fascinated by it.

item.title: After the Fireworks, Slowing Down for America's Next 250
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

After the Fireworks, Slowing Down for America's Next 250

Personal Perspective: What Hamilton can teach America about the next chapter.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • The cost of our modern rushing isn’t just stress, it’s our relationships.
  • Alexander Hamilton's "non-stop" life reveals both the power and the peril of speed.
  • To bridge our divides for the next 250 years, speed is not the answer, it's slowing down with one another.

The fireworks have ended, and America has settled back into the familiar rhythms and disagreements of everyday life. Before we move on, may I suggest something else?

Let’s pause.

We’re living through an era that rewards rushing. Yes, AI and other technologies make nearly everything faster, but there is a cost for our relationships, too. In civic life and at home, we prepare rebuttals before we’ve fully understood what someone is trying to say. We let labels replace curiosity.

Does living this way actually serve us? Looking back at this anniversary, I think Alexander Hamilton has something to teach us for the next 250.

A Man Ahead of His Time

In the song “Non-Stop” from the musical Hamilton, Lin-Manuel Miranda perfectly captured Alexander Hamilton. Hamilton wrote, argued, and fought as if he were “running out of time.” And that drive was central to his role in founding the country. Hamilton would fit comfortably into today’s world. We celebrate people who move quickly, produce a lot, and sleep little.

Much of that drive is worth celebrating. But anyone who has rushed an important family conversation or work decision knows that speed comes with tradeoffs.

The Costs of Speed

Hamilton’s relentless ambition strained the relationships around him. He neglected his marriage and son. Small disagreements became political feuds. Ultimately, his life ended in a duel fueled by reactive pride.

We see similar costs in our own relationships. We look down at our phones instead of at the people we love. We write off those with different political views. Increasingly, we ask AI for advice before asking a friend, or order from Amazon before asking a neighbor. I’ve seen these costs in my own life. I’ve said things I couldn’t take back to people I love. I’ve sent snippy emails to colleagues who were doing their best. I’ve sneered at people wearing the wrong T-shirt or hat.

The message I take from Hamilton, and one I explore more fully in Sometimes You Should Be Late: our fastest selves are not our wisest, and they are certainly not the ones most capable of healing relationships or a country.

A Slower America

Living in Washington, D.C., I felt the tension surrounding this anniversary. Some were eager to celebrate what’s beautiful about our country. Others wanted to leave town rather than celebrate what America looks like today. There wasn’t much room for nuance or slowness.

article continues after advertisement

Democracy is intentionally slow. Election cycles that can seem eternal and the arduous process of passing a law, immortalized by Schoolhouse Rock, aren’t flaws. While it may seem we are far from this ideal today, these processes allow room for deliberation, learning, and action to come from enduring values and compromise, rather than self-righteousness or reactivity.

The same is true in our relationships with our fellow Americans. Slowing down gives us space to recognize the fear or desire behind our own reaction, take a breath, and say, “I don’t see it that way. But help me understand how you do.” It gives us the chance to put down the phone and give our families at least as much attention as the latest outrage.

The Next 250

America has lived long enough to know that moving faster is not always the answer. Sure, urgency helped us fight off the British. But I’m not sure it’s the answer for the next 250. A less non-stop life gives us the chance to see our country and one another with more perspective. Not to become less frustrated by the gap between what America is and what it can be, but to stay with that first reaction long enough to respond from a wiser part of ourselves.
